title: Architecture and Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADR Process
author: Jordan Alvarez
content:
Summary

This consolidated standards document defines Redwood Inference's platform-level architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure (IaC) and networking, model-serving, observability, performance SLOs, and the ADR process. It supersedes earlier fragmentary guidelines and centralizes authorship and ownership so teams can ship consistent, secure, and observable inference services.

Goals
- Provide clear, actionable standards that enable predictable performance, security, and operability across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Reduce cognitive overhead for service teams by standardizing primitives (auth, schemas, metrics, alerts, deployment patterns).
- Ensure all major decisions are recorded with ADRs and have clear rollback/roll-forward procedures.

Principles
1. Developer-first: APIs and infra should be ergonomic for engineers while preserving production constraints (SLOs, security).
2. Observable by default: Every service must emit structured logs, distributed traces, and a minimum set of metrics.
3. Incremental and reversible change: Feature flags, canary deploys, and ADRs for non-trivial architecture changes.
4. Security and least privilege: Secrets, keys, and customer data must follow the security-and-compliance standards.
5. Measure everything: Decisions are validated with metrics, cost, and quality regressions.

1) API Standards
Purpose
Define consistent REST/JSON and RPC semantics across Redwood public and internal APIs to reduce integration bugs and improve client ergonomics.

Surface-level rules
- API types: Public (hosted API), Internal (service-to-service), Admin (control-plane). Each has defined auth and rate limit rules.
- Versioning: Use explicit version in the path (e.g., /v1/) for public APIs. Backwards-incompatible changes require a new major version.
- Idempotency: All mutating endpoints must accept idempotency-key where operations may be retried.
- Pagination: Use cursor-based pagination for large lists. Response envelope includes { data: [], next_cursor: string | null }.
- Error model: Use HTTP status codes. Body schema: {\"error\": {\"code\":\"<machine>\",\"message\":\"<human>\",\"details\": {}}}. Avoid exposing internal stack traces.
- Auth: OAuth2 bearer tokens for public APIs. Internal services use mTLS + short-lived JWT service tokens managed by platform identity.
- Rate limiting: Token-level rate limits for hosted API; service-level for internal endpoints. Return 429 with Retry-After.

Payload & schema rules
- Use snake_case for JSON fields in public APIs. Internal services may use snake_case or camelCase but prefer snake_case for consistency.
- Avoid deep nested objects (>3 levels); favor flat resource representation and small referenced sub-resources.
- Use OpenAPI schema for core public endpoints. Each service owning public endpoints must publish an OpenAPI document and a generated client in at least one language.

Backwards compatibility checklist (for maintainers)
1. Additive fields are safe.
2. Removing or renaming fields requires deprecation window (>= 90 days) and ADR for major public APIs.
3. Schema migration plan: provide validation tooling and rollout plan.

Example (error response)
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "model_not_found",
    "message": "Model 'redwood-1b' not found in region us-west-2",
    "details": {
      "requested_model": "redwood-1b"
    }
  }
}

2) Coding Standards
Purpose
Ensure readability, maintainability, and testability across Redwood codebases. These standards are minimum requirements; teams may adopt stricter rules.

Languages in use
- Python (service orchestration, SDKs), Go (performance-critical services), TypeScript (console and SDKs).

General rules
- Formatting and linting: All repos must enforce code formatting (black/isort for Python, gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, prettier/eslint for TypeScript) in CI.
- Typing: Use type annotations (mypy for Python, Go types, TypeScript strict mode).
- Testing: Minimum 80% unit-test coverage for core logic; critical paths must have integration tests. Tests run in CI with pre-merge gates.
- Commit message convention: Use conventional commits (type(scope): subject).
- Dependency policy: Follow security-and-compliance vulnerability scanning policy; pin direct dependencies and refresh quarterly.
- Repository layout: Services should follow the standard template (README.md, /cmd, /pkg, /internal for Go; /src, /tests for Python/TS).

Code review & ownership
- Every change must have at least one reviewer from the service team.
- Use CODEOWNERS to enforce approvers for critical paths.

3) Infrastructure (IaC & Networking) Standards
Purpose
Standardize cloud accounts, networking, and terraform modules to minimize blast radius and accelerate secure private deployments.

Cloud & accounts
- Account model: Separate accounts for prod, staging, and dev. Dedicated customer accounts for Private deployments when required.
- Resource tagging: All cloud resources must include tags: service, owner, environment, cost_center, created_by.

Terraform & IaC
- Module registry: Use the internal terraform module registry. Reuse modules for VPC, subnets, IAM, KMS, and EKS/GKE.
- Immutable infra: Prefer immutable infrastructure patterns (image baking) for runtime nodes.
- State management: Centralized remote state with locking (S3 + DynamoDB or equivalent).

Networking & security
- VPCs: Define standard CIDR allocations per environment. Avoid overlapping CIDRs for private deployments unless managed by VPN/NAT.
- Service communication: Use private subnets and service mesh where appropriate. mTLS mandatory for cross-account service calls.
- Secrets: Store secrets in KMS-backed secrets manager. No secrets in repo or logs.

Deployment & rollout patterns
1. CI builds artifacts; deploy to canary pool (5-10% traffic)
2. Monitor key metrics for 15 minutes
3. If green, gradual rollout to 25%, 50%, 100%
4. Support immediate rollback via previous artifact and feature flags

Runbook snippet (rolling deploy)
1. Trigger deployment via CI/CD pipeline: `ci deploy --service <service> --env staging`
2. Validate health checks and readiness endpoints `curl -f https://<svc>/healthz`
3. Promote canary after pass; otherwise rollback `ci rollback --service <service>`

4) Model-serving Standards
Purpose
Ensure model behaviors exposed via the Redwood runtime are consistent across hosting modes and that model onboarding and rollouts are auditable.

Model catalog & metadata
- Every model must be registered in the model catalog with metadata: name, version, architecture, quantization profile, max_seq_len, memory_estimate, input_signature, owner, allowed_regions.
- Model variants: Maintain compatibility matrix between variant types (float32, int8, int4-quantized). Runtime will prefer smallest variant that meets quality thresholds for cost-sensitive routes.

Versioning & rollouts
- Semantic versioning for model packages (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Backward-incompatible tokenizer or signature changes require MAJOR bump and ADR.
- Canary serving: Use shadow traffic and small-percentage canary traffic with per-model quality monitoring.

Serving config (example table)
- max_concurrent_requests: 200
- batch_size: dynamic (recommendation: 8-64 based on model)
- kv_cache_enabled: true
- kv_cache_ttl: 3600 (seconds)
- response_timeout_ms: 60000

Quality guardrails
- Baseline eval set: Each model must have a published eval set and periodic regression alerts (see applied-ml-and-evals/quality-guardrails).
- Regression thresholds: >5% degradation on primary metric triggers immediate rollback or mitigation.

Quantization & precision policy
- Use validated quantization profiles per model family. Profiles live in confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles.
- Performance-vs-quality tradeoffs must be captured in the model catalog entry.

5) Observability Standards
Purpose
All services must be observable to enable fast incident response and capacity planning. Observability includes metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, and alerting policies.

Minimum metrics (per service)
- request_count (counter) with labels: route, status_code, model, customer_tier
- request_latency_ms (histogram) with p50/p90/p95/p99 buckets
- token_emitted_count (counter) for LLM workloads
- batch_size_distribution (histogram)
- errors_total (counter) labeled by error_code

Tracing & logs
- Traces: Use W3C Trace Context. All incoming requests must propagate trace ids and emit a root trace spanning frontend -> runtime -> backend model host.
- Logs: Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, service, level, trace_id, span_id, request_id, user_id (if available), message. PII must be stripped or redacted.

Dashboards & alerts
- Standard dashboards: Per-service overview (traffic, latency, errors, cost), per-model dashboard (tokens/day, cost/1k tokens, quality regressions).
- Alerting thresholds (must have runbook links):
  - P1: error_rate > 5% for 5m OR p99 latency > 3x SLO for 5m -> page SRE on-call
  - P2: sustained increase in cost/unit > 30% week-over-week for 1d -> notify owner team
  - P3: degraded but recoverable performance (p95 above SLO) -> slack channel notification

6) Performance Standards and SLOs
Purpose
Define platform SLOs to set expectations for customers and to prioritize reliability work.

Platform SLOs (hosted API default)
- Availability: 99.95% (monthly uptime) for control-plane and critical inference endpoints
- Latency: p95 <= 1200ms for text-generation baseline (short prompts <= 256 tokens) under normal load; p99 <= 3000ms.
- Throughput: Per-GPU throughput targets documented in eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite.

Service SLO checklist
- Define SLI (metric), window (30d), target, and error budget. Store SLO config in the service repo under /observability/slo.yaml.
- SLO burn alerts: Notify owner at 25%, 50%, 75% burn. On 100% burn, open an incident and begin mitigation/reduction of traffic.

Load testing & benchmarking
- All services that affect customer-facing latency must be load-tested quarterly using the standard benchmark harness (eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite).
- Include representative traces and token distributions for realistic batching effects.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process
Purpose
Make architectural decisions discoverable and reversible. ADRs create a record for future engineers and provide context for trade-offs.

When to create an ADR
- Any decision that affects cross-team contracts (API changes, infra patterns), non-trivial security posture, or model-serving semantic changes must have an ADR.
- Small implementation choices (e.g., internal refactor) do not require ADRs unless they impact other teams.

ADR template (file in repo: /docs/adr/NNNN-title.md)
- Title: short descriptive name
- Status: proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated
- Date: YYYY-MM-DD
- Context: background and constraints
- Decision: what we decided and why
- Consequences: operational, cost, and compatibility implications
- Rollout plan: steps and metrics to evaluate success
- Owner: team and primary author

ADR lifecycle
1. Draft ADR and post to team mailing list and #architecture slack channel.
2. Reviewers: At least 2 reviewers from impacted teams; collect feedback for 7 calendar days.
3. If approved, change status to accepted and link to implementation PR(s).
4. If superseded, update ADR with link to new ADR and status = superseded.

Example ADR (short)
- Title: Standardize API error envelope
- Status: accepted
- Date: 2025-11-03
- Context: Different services returned inconsistent error payloads causing client parsing bugs
- Decision: Standardize on { error: { code, message, details }} and require OpenAPI examples
- Consequences: Minor client updates; improves client SDK ergonomics
- Rollout: 90-day deprecation window for non-conforming endpoints
- Owner: eng-developer-experience

Appendices
A. Ownership matrix (examples)
- API standards: eng-developer-experience
- IaC modules: eng-infra
- Runtime and kernels: eng-serving-runtime
- Observability & SLOs: eng-platform / eng-sre
- Model catalog & quantization profiles: applied-ml-and-evals

B. Example SLO YAML (slo.yaml)
```
name: hosted-api-latency
sli:
  metric: request_latency_ms_p95
  query: "histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le))"
window_days: 30
target: "1200ms"
error_budget: 0.005
owners:
  - team: eng-sre
  - team: eng-platform
```

C. Quick rollout checklist for API changes
1. Create feature branch, update OpenAPI schema, add migration notes.
2. Publish client patch in single language for smoke tests.
3. Deploy to staging; run contract tests and performance benchmarks.
4. Start canary (5% traffic) with health + regression checks for 1h.
5. Gradual rollout if green; otherwise roll back and open ADR if required.

D. References
- applied-ml-and-evals/quality-guardrails
- eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- security-and-compliance/incident-response-security
- eng-infra/terraform-and-iac

E. Contact & ownership
For questions about these standards or to propose changes, open a PR against this document or ping the architecture SIG in #architecture. Owners: Jordan Alvarez (architecture lead), eng-platform (standards steward).
